Fill in the gaps.

The Southport Attacks (2024)

atoms.b: On 29 July 2024, a 17-year-old ((stabbed)) three young girls at a dance class in Southport.
Within hours of the attack, ((false_information)) spread rapidly on social media claiming that the ((suspect)) was a Muslim asylum seeker who had arrived illegally by boat.
This was untrue: the attacker, Axel Rudakubana, was ((born)) in Cardiff to Rwandan parents and had lived in Britain his ((entire)) life.

Nevertheless, the misinformation triggered a wave of ((far-right_riots)) across England and Northern Ireland over the following days. Mosques, hotels housing asylum seekers and solicitors' offices were attacked.

instruction.text: Read the text. Decide whether the following statements are true or false.

atoms.text:
In a speech delivered in January 2025, Prime Minister Keir Starmer warned that Britain risked becoming an “island of strangers” if immigration was not brought under control.
He argued that unmanaged migration had damaged social cohesion—the sense of shared values and mutual trust that holds communities together—and announced plans to reduce net migration significantly.
atoms.sound: In a speech delivered in January 2025, Prime Minister Keir Starmer warned that Britain risked becoming an “island of strangers” if immigration was not brought under control. He argued that unmanaged migration had damaged social cohesion—the sense of shared values and mutual trust that holds communities together—and announced plans to reduce net migration significantly.

atoms.a: Starmer argued that unmanaged migration had damaged social cohesion.
Starmer announced plans to increase net migration over the following years.

wrong.text: Starmer announced plans to decrease net migration over the following years.

atoms.text: The phrase “island of strangers” provoked immediate controversy: supporters argued that Starmer was addressing a genuine concern felt by many communities across the country and that it was the responsibility of a government to manage migration in an orderly way.

atoms.a: Supporters believed that Starmer was responding to concerns about migration shared by many communities across the UK.

atoms.text: Critics, however, pointed out that the language echoed Enoch Powell's notorious 1968 “Rivers of Blood” speech and that framing migrants as strangers dehumanised people who had contributed enormously to British society. Some commentators noted the particular irony of the phrase given that Britain's NHS, transport network and care sector remain heavily dependent on migrant workers.

hint.text: Enoch Powell (1912–1998) was a Conservative British politician and Member of Parliament. In 1968, he delivered a speech in Birmingham in which he argued fiercely against immigration from Commonwealth countries and warned of violent social conflict to come. The speech was immediately condemned as racist and inflammatory.

atoms.a: Critics of Starmer pointed out that Britain's NHS, transport network and care sector are barely dependent on migrant workers.

wrong.text: They pointed out that Britain's NHS, transport network and care sector are heavily dependent on migrant workers.

instruction.text:
Fill in the gaps.

The ongoing debate

atoms.b: Immigration remains one of the most contested issues in British politics, as people hold very strong and opposing ((views)).
Critics argue that rapid demographic change makes it harder to maintain a shared ((national_identity)).
((Supporters)) of open migration say that migrants fill critical gaps in the workforce, especially in healthcare and construction.
Britain's ageing population means the country needs working-age ((immigrants)) to sustain its pension system.
Many argue that pressure on public services is actually the result of years of ((underinvestment)), not immigration.
Supporters say that ((cultural_diversity)) has enriched British life in countless ways.
At the heart of the debate is a question about identity and ((belonging)). What does it really mean to be British?

atoms.text: Britain has always been shaped by the movement of people — from Roman soldiers and Viking settlers to Huguenot refugees, Caribbean people and Ugandan Asians. The tensions that flared in Southport's aftermath and the controversy surrounding Starmer's words are not new. They are a chapter in a long, unfinished story about identity, belonging and what kind of society Britain wants to be.
